screens.title: Package Management and Software Installation
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll learn the practical skills you need to install and manage software on Raspberry Pi OS. You will learn how the apt package manager keeps a list of available packages, how to refresh that list and apply upgrades, and how to install or remove packages cleanly. We also cover how to install downloaded Debian packages with dpkg, and how system packages differ from Python packages installed with pip. Finally, you'll learn simple ways to locate programs and read their built-in documentation with which, whereis, man and the help flag. These are not just commands to memorize — they are the routines that keep a Pi healthy and maintainable. For example, updating the package list before an install helps avoid broken dependencies; reading a manual page helps you pick the right option without guessing. By the end of this lesson you will have a repeatable flow: update, install, verify, and tidy up. Think about a time you installed a program and saw a missing library: these steps will help you diagnose and fix that problem quickly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives define the practical skills you'll practice. First, you'll use apt to update the package list and to install, remove, and upgrade packages. This matters because package lists tell your system what versions are available; without updating you may install an older or incompatible build. Second, you'll understand the difference between system packages and Python packages. System packages affect the whole operating system and are managed by apt, while Python packages installed with pip are scoped to Python environments and can cause conflicts if mixed carelessly. Third, you'll install software from source or from downloaded. deb files and learn to resolve dependency issues using dpkg and apt. Installing a. deb may be necessary for vendor tools that aren't in the official repositories. Fourth, you'll locate commands with which and whereis and read manual pages with man or quick help with the help flag. Knowing where an executable lives and reading its documentation will help you automate tasks and troubleshoot problems. Each objective includes hands-on steps so you can verify competency by completing a short activity on your Pi.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.eyebrow: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practical verification. You'll update your package list and then upgrade installed software so you can see how apt reports upgrades and requires confirmation. You will install a small utility such as htop and verify it runs, then remove it and use autoremove to clear orphaned dependencies. You'll install a downloaded. deb with dpkg and then resolve any missing libraries using apt --fix-broken. You'll also run which to print the path to an executable and use man to read its manual, then press q to quit the viewer. These verification steps matter because a successful install is more than a green success line — it means you can run the program, find where it lives, and remove it cleanly when it's no longer needed. Try to notice the difference between package manager output that updates lists and output that actually changes installed files, then reflect on how that distinction affects safe maintenance of a Pi.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Practice & Verify
Verification checklist
  • Refresh package index and confirm no errors during update.
  • Install htop and open it to observe processes.
  • Remove neofetch and run autoremove to tidy dependencies.
  • Install a .deb and run apt --fix-broken if needed.

Common quick checks
Did the install print errors?
Can you run the program?
Was a new binary created in /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin?
Are leftover packages present after removal?
Micro-mnemonic

screens.title: What is apt and how repositories work
screens.narratorSegment: Apt, the Advanced Package Tool, is the package manager used on Raspberry Pi OS. Think of apt as a catalogue system: repositories are remote indexes that list pre-built packages, their versions and dependencies. When you run an update, apt refreshes its local catalogue so the system knows which package versions are available. Installing a package with apt fetches the pre-compiled files and places binaries, libraries and metadata in the right system locations. This approach avoids building from source and ensures consistent installation paths across machines. An example: installing a system monitor like htop uses apt to download a tested binary and any libraries it needs; you don't compile anything yourself. A common misconception is that apt both downloads and updates packages without user control; in reality apt separates listing available versions from actually upgrading installed files — update refreshes the list, upgrade performs file changes. Why that separation matters: you can inspect changes before applying upgrades, avoiding unexpected modifications. As a takeaway, repositories provide trusted, curated software; apt is the local tool that consults them and manages package lifecycle on the Pi.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › What is apt
Definition

Apt is the package management interface that consults remote repositories containing pre-compiled packages and dependency information. It automates download, install, upgrade and removal operations for system software.

How repositories help
  • Provide curated and versioned packages for consistent installs.
  • Supply dependency metadata so apt can fetch required libraries.
  • Allow centralized security updates through apt upgrade.
Key Takeaway

Apt relies on repositories to supply tested packages; updating the list is the first step before installing or upgrading.

Terminal example (visual only)
$ sudo apt update
Hit:1 archive ...
Reading package lists... Done
This output tells apt it refreshed the index. No packages were installed yet; the system now knows the latest available versions.
Analogy
Think of repositories as an app store catalogue and apt as the client that reads that catalogue to download and install approved apps for the system.

screens.title: apt update vs apt upgrade
screens.narratorSegment: It is common to see update and upgrade used together, but they do different things. The update step refreshes the local package index so the system learns about the newest package versions available from repositories. No installed files change during this step; apt only updates metadata. The upgrade step applies available newer versions to packages you already have installed. Running upgrade without updating first risks installing older versions or missing recent releases. A standard safe workflow is to run update, inspect output for errors, and then run upgrade. You can combine them in a single line when you are sure, but combining uses logical sequencing: the second runs only if the first succeeded. For example, using an automatic yes flag will accept prompts; use that with care because it bypasses opportunity to review changes. A common misconception is that update downloads package files — it does not. One concrete example: before installing a new program, update so apt can fetch the package from the latest index. Now, try to recall: does update change installed binaries, or does upgrade? That understanding is crucial for safe system maintenance.

keyIdea.title: Two-step safety
keyIdea.text: Update refreshes indexes; upgrade changes files. Do update first to ensure you apply the latest available upgrades.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Update vs Upgrade
Step definitions
  • Update: refresh the package index so apt knows available versions.
  • Upgrade: apply available newer versions for installed packages.
  • Combine: use logical sequencing so upgrade runs only if update succeeds.
Common command patterns (visual)
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
The && operator runs the second command only if the first completes successfully. The -y flag answers yes to prompts automatically.
Illustrative scenario

Imagine you want to install an updated driver. If you skip update, apt may use an old index and install a package that conflicts with other packages. Running update first ensures apt will consider the correct dependency graph before upgrading.

Common mistake

Treating update as an upgrade. Remember: update refreshes metadata; upgrade changes installed files.

Check your understanding
Which step should you run before installing a new package and why?

screens.title: Installing and removing packages with apt
screens.narratorSegment: Installing and removing packages with apt is a routine you will use daily. To install software, the typical pattern is to run an install command with administrator privileges and list the packages you want. For example, installing a text editor and a system monitor together saves time. When removing software, apt remove uninstalls the package binaries but leaves configuration files behind; using purge removes those configuration files as well. After repeated installs and removals, unused dependencies can accumulate — apt autoremove clears libraries that are no longer required by any installed package. A concrete hands-on example is to install htop, open it to observe processes, then remove it and run autoremove to confirm no leftover libraries remain. A common misconception is that remove always reclaims all disk space; it does not remove configuration files or orphaned packages. Your takeaway: pick the right command for the goal — remove for uninstall, purge to remove configs, and autoremove to reclaim unused dependencies. Installing and removing packages with apt means use install to add packages, remove to uninstall binary files, purge to remove configuration, and autoremove to clean orphaned dependencies.. In practical terms, install multiple packages, remove or purge, and tidy dependencies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use install to add packages, remove to uninstall binary files, purge to remove configuration, and autoremove to clean orphaned dependencies.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Install & Remove
Typical install workflow
  1. Refresh the package index with update.
  2. Install desired packages with install and list names separated by spaces.
  3. Verify the program runs and find its location.
Removal options
  • remove: uninstalls binaries but keeps configuration files.
  • purge: removes package and configuration files.
  • autoremove: deletes dependencies no longer required.
Key Takeaway

Choose remove or purge depending on whether you want to keep configuration, and run autoremove to reclaim space.

Terminal demo (visual)
$ sudo apt install nano htop
...
$ htop  # run to check
$ sudo apt remove htop
$ sudo apt autoremove
Practice installing multiple packages in a single command, then run the program and remove it to observe cleanup behavior.
Common mistake
Expecting complete cleanup without purge. If configuration files remain, use purge to remove them as well.

screens.title: Installing .deb files and using dpkg
screens.narratorSegment: Sometimes software is distributed as a Debian package file with a. deb extension. This is common when vendors provide builds that are not present in the official repositories. To install such a file you can use the dpkg tool, which places files directly on the system from the package you downloaded. However dpkg does not automatically resolve missing dependencies from repositories. If dpkg reports missing packages, you can run apt --fix-broken install to download and install the dependencies and finish the install cleanly. A concrete example: you download vendor-tool. deb, run the dpkg installer, and see an error about missing libraries. Running apt --fix-broken install will fetch the needed packages from your configured repositories and complete the installation. A common misconception is that dpkg replaces apt — it does not. dpkg performs the low-level unpack and register step for a specific package, while apt integrates with repositories to resolve and fetch dependent packages. Your takeaway: use dpkg to install a downloaded. deb and then use apt to repair or satisfy missing dependencies. Installing .deb files and using dpkg means use dpkg to install a downloaded .deb, then run apt --fix-broken install to fetch and install any missing dependencies.. In practical terms, when to use downloaded packages and how to repair broken installs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › .deb & dpkg
When to use .deb files

Use a downloaded .deb when the software vendor provides a package not available in the repositories, or when you require a specific build version.

Repairing with apt

If dpkg reports missing dependencies, run apt --fix-broken install to let apt fetch and install the required packages from your repositories.

Common mistake

Relying on dpkg alone for dependency resolution. Always follow with apt to fix and fetch missing libraries.

Terminal sequence (visual)
$ sudo dpkg -i package-name.deb
(installation output)
# if errors about missing packages
$ sudo apt --fix-broken install
Follow the dpkg install with apt to resolve dependencies. This two-step flow avoids broken packages on the system.
Analogy
Think of dpkg as unpacking a box you got in the mail. If the box needs extra parts, apt fetches those parts from the store so the item works correctly.

screens.title: Dependencies and the role of apt --fix-broken
screens.narratorSegment: Dependencies are other packages a program needs to run. When you install a package, apt normally ensures those dependencies are also installed. When you use lower-level tools like dpkg to install a. deb, apt may not have automatically fetched those dependencies and dpkg will report them. The apt --fix-broken install command instructs apt to examine the package database, find missing dependencies, and download and install them from configured repositories. A concrete troubleshooting scenario: after a dpkg install you see a message that certain libraries are not present. Running apt --fix-broken install retrieves those libraries and completes the installation without reinstalling the original. deb. A common misconception is to attempt manual downloads for each missing library; this increases risk and is error-prone. Instead, let apt resolve the dependency graph because it understands package relationships and versions. As a takeaway, when an install fails due to missing dependencies, run apt --fix-broken install rather than attempting piecemeal fixes. Dependencies and the role of apt --fix-broken means use apt --fix-broken install to let the package manager resolve missing dependencies and complete installs triggered by dpkg.. In practical terms, how to recognize and recover from missing libraries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fix broken installs
keyIdea.text: Use apt --fix-broken install to let the package manager resolve missing dependencies and complete installs triggered by dpkg.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Dependencies & Repair
What are dependencies?

Dependencies are other packages or libraries that a program needs. Apt uses dependency metadata to fetch required packages automatically when installing from repositories.

Repair command

Running apt --fix-broken install instructs apt to examine broken package states and download any missing dependencies so the system returns to a consistent state.

Key Takeaway

When dpkg reports missing libraries, use apt --fix-broken install to let the package manager resolve and fetch the missing pieces.

Troubleshooting example
You install a .deb and see dependency errors. Instead of manually locating packages, run the repair command to fetch the correct versions from your repositories and ensure compatibility.
Pro tip
Run apt update before running fix-broken so apt can find the required dependency packages in the freshest index.
Check your understanding
Why is relying on apt to resolve dependencies safer than downloading libraries manually?

screens.title: apt versus pip
screens.narratorSegment: A clear distinction exists between system package managers like apt and language-specific installers like pip. Apt manages system packages: these are pre-compiled applications and libraries that integrate with the operating system, install to system directories, and may be shared by multiple programs. Pip installs Python packages and libraries into Python environments; these packages are meant for use by Python programs and can be installed per user or per project. A concrete example: installing a command-line tool with apt makes it available system-wide under standard paths, whereas installing a Python library with pip makes it importable from Python code but might not provide a system executable unless the package explicitly installs an entry point. A common pitfall is mixing pip and apt for the same library; you can end up with conflicting versions or shadowing. When you need a Python-only library for a project, prefer pip inside a virtual environment; when a shared, system-level binary is required, prefer apt. As a takeaway, choose the tool based on scope: apt for system-level packages, pip for Python-specific dependencies. apt versus pip means apt manages system-wide packages; pip manages python packages. avoid mixing them for the same dependency to prevent conflicts.. In practical terms, why system packages and python packages are managed separately. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › apt vs pip
System packages (apt)
Installed system-wide, placed in standard paths, and managed by the OS-level package manager. Suitable for shared utilities and core libraries.
Python packages (pip)
Installed into Python environments; best used inside virtual environments for project isolation to avoid clashing with system packages.
Common mistake

Installing a Python package system-wide with pip can overwrite system-managed files and create conflicts. Prefer virtual environments for project dependencies.

Concrete scenario

If you need a Python library for a single project, create a virtual environment and use pip there. If you need a system tool available to all users, install it with apt so it integrates with system paths and service managers.

Quick rule
Scope decides the tool: system-wide → apt; project-specific Python → pip (inside virtual env).
Check your understanding
When should you prefer apt over pip? Answer by describing scope and sharing requirements.

screens.title: Find commands and read documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Finding where a command lives and reading its documentation are essential troubleshooting skills. The which command prints the path to the executable that will run when you invoke a command name. For example, which Python three typically outputs a full path such as /usr/bin/Python three. The whereis command returns common locations for binaries, source, and man pages, giving a broader view. To learn how to use a command, man shows the manual page with detailed options; press q to quit when finished. If no man page exists, most commands support a help flag that prints usage and common options. A practical example: if a script fails complaining about a missing executable, run which to confirm the path, then run man to read available options or behaviour. A common misconception is that which and whereis always agree — they can differ because which shows the command chosen by your shell PATH, while whereis searches common directories. As a takeaway, use these tools together: locate the executable with which, broaden the search with whereis, and consult man or help to understand the command's options.

Locate commands

Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Hands-on Activity

In this chapter we'll learn the practical skills you need to install and manage software on Raspberry Pi OS. You will learn how the apt package manager keeps a list of available packages, how to refresh that list and apply upgrades, and how to install or remove packages cleanly. We also cover how to install downloaded Debian packages with dpkg, and how system packages differ from Python packages installed with pip. Finally, you'll learn simple ways to locate programs and read their built-in documentation with which, whereis, man and the help flag. These are not just commands to memorize — they are the routines that keep a Pi healthy and maintainable. For example, updating the package list before an install helps avoid broken dependencies; reading a manual page helps you pick the right option without guessing. By the end of this lesson you will have a repeatable flow: update, install, verify, and tidy up. Think about a time you installed a program and saw a missing library: these steps will help you diagnose and fix that problem quickly.

These objectives define the practical skills you'll practice. First, you'll use apt to update the package list and to install, remove, and upgrade packages. This matters because package lists tell your system what versions are available; without updating you may install an older or incompatible build. Second, you'll understand the difference between system packages and Python packages. System packages affect the whole operating system and are managed by apt, while Python packages installed with pip are scoped to Python environments and can cause conflicts if mixed carelessly. Third, you'll install software from source or from downloaded. deb files and learn to resolve dependency issues using dpkg and apt. Installing a. deb may be necessary for vendor tools that aren't in the official repositories. Fourth, you'll locate commands with which and whereis and read manual pages with man or quick help with the help flag. Knowing where an executable lives and reading its documentation will help you automate tasks and troubleshoot problems. Each objective includes hands-on steps so you can verify competency by completing a short activity on your Pi.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical verification. You'll update your package list and then upgrade installed software so you can see how apt reports upgrades and requires confirmation. You will install a small utility such as htop and verify it runs, then remove it and use autoremove to clear orphaned dependencies. You'll install a downloaded. deb with dpkg and then resolve any missing libraries using apt --fix-broken. You'll also run which to print the path to an executable and use man to read its manual, then press q to quit the viewer. These verification steps matter because a successful install is more than a green success line — it means you can run the program, find where it lives, and remove it cleanly when it's no longer needed. Try to notice the difference between package manager output that updates lists and output that actually changes installed files, then reflect on how that distinction affects safe maintenance of a Pi.

Apt, the Advanced Package Tool, is the package manager used on Raspberry Pi OS. Think of apt as a catalogue system: repositories are remote indexes that list pre-built packages, their versions and dependencies. When you run an update, apt refreshes its local catalogue so the system knows which package versions are available. Installing a package with apt fetches the pre-compiled files and places binaries, libraries and metadata in the right system locations. This approach avoids building from source and ensures consistent installation paths across machines. An example: installing a system monitor like htop uses apt to download a tested binary and any libraries it needs; you don't compile anything yourself. A common misconception is that apt both downloads and updates packages without user control; in reality apt separates listing available versions from actually upgrading installed files — update refreshes the list, upgrade performs file changes. Why that separation matters: you can inspect changes before applying upgrades, avoiding unexpected modifications. As a takeaway, repositories provide trusted, curated software; apt is the local tool that consults them and manages package lifecycle on the Pi.

It is common to see update and upgrade used together, but they do different things. The update step refreshes the local package index so the system learns about the newest package versions available from repositories. No installed files change during this step; apt only updates metadata. The upgrade step applies available newer versions to packages you already have installed. Running upgrade without updating first risks installing older versions or missing recent releases. A standard safe workflow is to run update, inspect output for errors, and then run upgrade. You can combine them in a single line when you are sure, but combining uses logical sequencing: the second runs only if the first succeeded. For example, using an automatic yes flag will accept prompts; use that with care because it bypasses opportunity to review changes. A common misconception is that update downloads package files — it does not. One concrete example: before installing a new program, update so apt can fetch the package from the latest index. Now, try to recall: does update change installed binaries, or does upgrade? That understanding is crucial for safe system maintenance.

Installing and removing packages with apt is a routine you will use daily. To install software, the typical pattern is to run an install command with administrator privileges and list the packages you want. For example, installing a text editor and a system monitor together saves time. When removing software, apt remove uninstalls the package binaries but leaves configuration files behind; using purge removes those configuration files as well. After repeated installs and removals, unused dependencies can accumulate — apt autoremove clears libraries that are no longer required by any installed package. A concrete hands-on example is to install htop, open it to observe processes, then remove it and run autoremove to confirm no leftover libraries remain. A common misconception is that remove always reclaims all disk space; it does not remove configuration files or orphaned packages. Your takeaway: pick the right command for the goal — remove for uninstall, purge to remove configs, and autoremove to reclaim unused dependencies. Installing and removing packages with apt means use install to add packages, remove to uninstall binary files, purge to remove configuration, and autoremove to clean orphaned dependencies.. In practical terms, install multiple packages, remove or purge, and tidy dependencies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Sometimes software is distributed as a Debian package file with a. deb extension. This is common when vendors provide builds that are not present in the official repositories. To install such a file you can use the dpkg tool, which places files directly on the system from the package you downloaded. However dpkg does not automatically resolve missing dependencies from repositories. If dpkg reports missing packages, you can run apt --fix-broken install to download and install the dependencies and finish the install cleanly. A concrete example: you download vendor-tool. deb, run the dpkg installer, and see an error about missing libraries. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The apt --fix-broken install command instructs apt to examine the package database, find missing dependencies, and download and install them from configured repositories.
